**[RISC OS](/wiki/RISC_OS "RISC OS")**, the computer [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") developed by [Acorn Computers](/wiki/Acorn_Computers "Acorn Computers") for their [ARM](/wiki/ARM_architecture "ARM architecture")-based [Acorn Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") range, was originally released in 1987 as *Arthur 0.20*, and soon followed by *Arthur 0.30*, and *Arthur 1.20*. The next version, *Arthur 2*, became *RISC OS 2* and was completed in September 1988 and made available in April 1989. *RISC OS 3* was released with the very earliest version of the A5000 in 1991 and contained a series of new features. By 1996 RISC OS had been shipped on over 500,000 systems.[[1]](#cite_note-chrisacorns-1)

*RISC OS 4* was released by [RISCOS Ltd](/wiki/RISCOS_Ltd "RISCOS Ltd") (ROL) in July 1999, based on the continued development of OS 3.8. ROL had in March 1999 licensed the rights to RISC OS from Element 14 (the renamed Acorn) and eventually from the new owner, [Pace Micro Technology](/wiki/Pace_Micro_Technology "Pace Micro Technology"). According to the company, over 6,400 copies of OS 4.02 on ROM were sold up until production was ceased in mid-2005.

*RISC OS Select* was launched in May 2001 by ROL. This is a subscription scheme allowing users access to the latest OS updates. These upgrades are released as soft-loadable [ROM images](/wiki/ROM_image "ROM image"), separate to the ROM where the boot OS is stored, and are loaded at boot time. *Select 1* was shipped in May 2002, with *Select 2* following in November 2002 and the final release of *Select 3* in June 2004. ROL released the ROM based OS 4.39 the same month, dubbed *RISC OS Adjust* as a play on the RISC OS GUI convention of calling the three mouse buttons 'Select', 'Menu' and 'Adjust'. ROL sold its 500th Adjust ROM in early 2006.

*RISC OS Six* was also announced in October 2006 by ROL. This is the next generation of their stream of the operating system. The first product to be launched under the name was the continuation of the Select scheme, *Select 4*. A beta-version of OS 6, Preview 1 (*Select 4i1*), was available in 2007 as a free download to all subscribers to the Select scheme, while in April 2009 the final release of *Select 5* was shipped. The latest release of RISC OS from ROL is *Select 6i1*, shipped in December 2009.

The OS was designed in the [United Kingdom](/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") by [Acorn](/wiki/Acorn_Computers_Ltd "Acorn Computers Ltd") for the [32-bit](/wiki/32-bit "32-bit") ARM based [Acorn Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes"), and released in its first version in 1987, as the [Arthur](/wiki/Arthur_(operating_system) "Arthur (operating system)") operating system.
The first public release of the OS was *Arthur 1.20* in June 1987.[[2]](#cite_note-History310-2)

The OS was designed in the [United Kingdom](/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") by [Acorn](/wiki/Acorn_Computers_Ltd "Acorn Computers Ltd") for the [32-bit](/wiki/32-bit "32-bit") ARM based [Acorn Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes"), and released in its first version in 1987, as the [Arthur](/wiki/Arthur_(operating_system) "Arthur (operating system)") operating system.
The first public release of the OS was *Arthur 1.20* in June 1987.[[2]](#cite_note-History310-2)

It was bundled with a desktop [graphical user interface](/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") (GUI), which mostly comprises [assembly language](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language") software modules,[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] and the Desktop module itself being written in [BBC BASIC](/wiki/BBC_BASIC "BBC BASIC").[[3]](#cite_note-pcw_1987-3) It features a colour-scheme typically described as "[technicolor](/wiki/Technicolor "Technicolor")".[[4]](#cite_note-osnewsDock-4)

The graphical desktop runs on top of a [command-line](/wiki/Command_line_interface "Command line interface") driven operating system which owes much to Acorn's earlier [MOS](/wiki/Acorn_MOS "Acorn MOS") operating system for its [BBC Micro](/wiki/BBC_Micro "BBC Micro") range of [8-bit](/wiki/8-bit "8-bit") microcomputers.[[5]](#cite_note-acornpov-5)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
The graphical desktop runs on top of a [command-line](/wiki/Command_line_interface "Command line interface") driven operating system which owes much to Acorn's earlier [MOS](/wiki/Acorn_MOS "Acorn MOS") operating system for its [BBC Micro](/wiki/BBC_Micro "BBC Micro") range of [8-bit](/wiki/8-bit "8-bit") microcomputers.[[5]](#cite_note-acornpov-5)

Arthur, as originally conceived, was intended to deliver similar functionality to the operating system for the [BBC Master](/wiki/BBC_Master "BBC Master") series of computers, [MOS](/wiki/Acorn_MOS "Acorn MOS"), as a reaction to the fact that a more advanced operating system research project ([ARX](/wiki/ARX_(operating_system) "ARX (operating system)")) would not be ready in time for the [Archimedes](/wiki/Archimedes_(computer) "Archimedes (computer)").[[5]](#cite_note-acornpov-5)

The Arthur project team, led by Paul Fellows, was given just five months to develop it entirely from the ground up—with the directive "just make it like the BBC micro". It was intended as a stop-gap until the operating system which Acorn had under development ([ARX](/wiki/ARX_(operating_system) "ARX (operating system)")) could be completed. However, the latter was delayed time and again, and was eventually dropped when it became apparent that the Arthur development could be extended to have a window manager and full desktop environment. Also, it was small enough to run on the first 512K machines with only a floppy disc, whereas ARX required 4 megabytes and a hard drive.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

The OS development was carried out using a prototype ARM-based system connected to a BBC computer, before moving onto the prototype [Acorn Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") the A500.[[6]](#cite_note-chrisacornsA500-6)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
The OS development was carried out using a prototype ARM-based system connected to a BBC computer, before moving onto the prototype [Acorn Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") the A500.[[6]](#cite_note-chrisacornsA500-6)

Arthur was not a multitasking operating system, but offered support for adding application-level [cooperative multitasking](/wiki/Cooperative_multitasking "Cooperative multitasking").[[7]](#cite_note-pountain198710-7) No other version of the operating system was released externally, but internally the development of the desktop and window management continued, with the addition of a cooperative multitasking system, implemented by Neil Raine, which used the memory management hardware to swap-out one task, and bring in another between call-and-return from the `Wimp_Poll` call that applications were obliged to make to get messages under the desktop. Reminiscent of a similar technique employed by [MultiFinder](/wiki/MultiFinder "MultiFinder") on the [Apple Macintosh](/wiki/Apple_Macintosh "Apple Macintosh"),[[8]](#cite_note-byte198711-8) this transformed a single-application-at-a-time system into one that could operate a full multi-tasking desktop. This transformation took place at version 1.6 though it was not made public until released, with the name change from Arthur to RISC OS, as version 2.0.[[9]](#cite_note-fellows-9)

(A few titles will not work, however, because they used undocumented features, side effects or in a few cases APIs that became deprecated).[*[original research?](/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research "Wikipedia:No original research")*]

title: History of RISC OS
text:
RISC OS was a rapid development of Arthur 1.2 after the failure of the [ARX](/wiki/ARX_(operating_system) "ARX (operating system)") project.[[5]](#cite_note-acornpov-5) Given growing dissatisfaction with various bugs and limitations with Arthur, testing of what was then known as Arthur 2 was apparently ongoing during 1988 with selected software houses.[[11]](#cite_note-acornuser198807-11)

At this stage, Computer Concepts, who had been prolific developers for the BBC Micro and who had begun software development for the Archimedes, had already initiated a rival operating system project, Impulse, to support their own applications (including the desktop publishing application that would eventually become [Impression](/wiki/Impression_(software) "Impression (software)")), stating that Arthur did not meet the "hundreds of requirements" involved including "true multi-tasking".[[12]](#cite_note-acornuser198806-12) Such an operating system was to be offered free of charge with the planned application packages,[[11]](#cite_note-acornuser198807-11) but with the release of RISC OS and Computer Concepts acknowledging that RISC OS "overcomes the old problems with Arthur", the applications were to be able to run under either RISC OS or Impulse.[[13]](#cite_note-acornuser198901-13) Impression was eventually released as a RISC OS application.[[14]](#cite_note-acornuser199005-14)

Ultimately, Arthur 2 was renamed to *RISC OS*, and was first sold as *RISC OS 2.00* in April 1989.[[15]](#cite_note-acornuser198902-15)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
At this stage, Computer Concepts, who had been prolific developers for the BBC Micro and who had begun software development for the Archimedes, had already initiated a rival operating system project, Impulse, to support their own applications (including the desktop publishing application that would eventually become [Impression](/wiki/Impression_(software) "Impression (software)")), stating that Arthur did not meet the "hundreds of requirements" involved including "true multi-tasking".[[12]](#cite_note-acornuser198806-12) Such an operating system was to be offered free of charge with the planned application packages,[[11]](#cite_note-acornuser198807-11) but with the release of RISC OS and Computer Concepts acknowledging that RISC OS "overcomes the old problems with Arthur", the applications were to be able to run under either RISC OS or Impulse.[[13]](#cite_note-acornuser198901-13) Impression was eventually released as a RISC OS application.[[14]](#cite_note-acornuser199005-14)

Ultimately, Arthur 2 was renamed to *RISC OS*, and was first sold as *RISC OS 2.00* in April 1989.[[15]](#cite_note-acornuser198902-15)

The operating system implements [co-operative multitasking](/wiki/Co-operative_multitasking "Co-operative multitasking") with some limitations but is not [multi-threaded](/wiki/Thread_(computer_science) "Thread (computer science)"). It uses the [ADFS](/wiki/Advanced_Disc_Filing_System "Advanced Disc Filing System") file system for both floppy and hard disc access. It ran from a 512 [KB](/wiki/Kilobyte "Kilobyte") set of [ROMs](/wiki/Read-only_memory "Read-only memory"). The [WIMP](/wiki/WIMP_(computing) "WIMP (computing)") interface offers all the standard features and fixes many of the [bugs](/wiki/Computer_bug "Computer bug") that had hindered Arthur. It lacks [virtual memory](/wiki/Virtual_memory "Virtual memory") and extensive [memory protection](/wiki/Memory_protection "Memory protection") (applications are protected from each other, but many functions have to be implemented as 'modules' which have full access to the memory). At the time of release, the main advantage of the OS was its ROM; it booted very quickly and while it was easy to crash, it was impossible to permanently break the OS from software. Its high performance was due to much of the system being written in [ARM](/wiki/ARM_architecture "ARM architecture") [assembly language](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

The OS was designed with users in mind, rather than OS designers.[[16]](#cite_note-Stoye1990-16) It is organised as a relatively small kernel which defines a standard software interface to which extension modules are required to conform. Much of the system's functionality is implemented in modules coded in the ROM, though these can be supplanted by more evolved versions loaded into [RAM](/wiki/Random_Access_Memory "Random Access Memory"). Among the kernel facilities are a general mechanism, named the callback handler, which allows a supervisor module to perform process multiplexing. This facility is used by a module forming part of the standard editor program to provide a [terminal emulator](/wiki/Terminal_emulator "Terminal emulator") window for console applications. The same approach made it possible for advanced users to implement modules giving RISC OS the ability to do [pre-emptive multitasking](/wiki/Pre-emptive_multitasking "Pre-emptive multitasking").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

title: History of RISC OS
text:
## RISC OS 3

RISC OS 3 introduced a number of new features,[[18]](#cite_note-RO3MarketingQandA-18) including multitasking *Filer* operations, applications and fonts in ROM, no limit on number of open windows, ability to move windows off screen, safe [shutdown](/wiki/Shutdown_(computing) "Shutdown (computing)"), the *Pinboard*, grouping of icon bar icons, up to 128 tasks, native ability to read [MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS") format discs and use named hard discs. Improved [configuration](/wiki/Configuration_file "Configuration file") was also included, by way of multiple windows to change the settings.[[18]](#cite_note-RO3MarketingQandA-18)

*RISC OS 3.00* was released with the very earliest version of the A5000 in 1991; it is almost four times the size of RISC OS 2 and runs from a 2 [MB](/wiki/Mebibyte "Mebibyte") ROM. It improves multitasking and also places some of the more popular base applications in the ROM. RISC OS 3.00 had several bugs and was replaced by RISC OS 3.1 a few months later; the upgraded ROMs were supplied for the cost of postage.

## Demise of Acorn Computers Ltd

Acorn officially halted work in all areas except [set-top boxes](/wiki/Set-top_box "Set-top box") in January 1999 and the company was renamed [Element 14](/wiki/Element_14_(company) "Element 14 (company)")[[21]](#cite_note-Companies_House_"Acorn_Computers_Limited"-21) (the 14th element of the [periodic table](/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table") being [silicon](/wiki/Silicon "Silicon")) with a new goal to become purely a Silicon design business (like the previous very successful spin off of ARM from Acorn in 1990). RISC OS development was halted during the development of OS 4.0 for the RiscPC 2 ("[Phoebe 2100](/wiki/Phoebe_2100 "Phoebe 2100")"), whose completion was also cancelled. A beta version, OS 3.8 ("Ursula") for the original RiscPC, had previously been released to developers. The project code names of Phoebe (for the hardware), Ursula (for the software) and Chandler (for the graphics processor chip) were taken from the names of characters in the TV series *[Friends](/wiki/Friends "Friends")* (Phoebe and Ursula were twin sisters in the series).

Acorn officially halted work in all areas except [set-top boxes](/wiki/Set-top_box "Set-top box") in January 1999 and the company was renamed [Element 14](/wiki/Element_14_(company) "Element 14 (company)")[[21]](#cite_note-Companies_House_"Acorn_Computers_Limited"-21) (the 14th element of the [periodic table](/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table") being [silicon](/wiki/Silicon "Silicon")) with a new goal to become purely a Silicon design business (like the previous very successful spin off of ARM from Acorn in 1990). RISC OS development was halted during the development of OS 4.0 for the RiscPC 2 ("[Phoebe 2100](/wiki/Phoebe_2100 "Phoebe 2100")"), whose completion was also cancelled. A beta version, OS 3.8 ("Ursula") for the original RiscPC, had previously been released to developers. The project code names of Phoebe (for the hardware), Ursula (for the software) and Chandler (for the graphics processor chip) were taken from the names of characters in the TV series *[Friends](/wiki/Friends "Friends")* (Phoebe and Ursula were twin sisters in the series).

This led to a number of rescue efforts to try to keep the Acorn desktop computer business alive. Acorn held discussions with many interested parties, and eventually agreed to exclusively licence RISC OS to RISCOS Ltd, which was formed from a consortium of dealers, developers and end-users. Pace purchased the rights to use and develop NCOS.
There were also a number of projects to bring the advantages of the RISC Operating System to other platforms by the creation of the [ROX Desktop](/wiki/ROX_Desktop "ROX Desktop") to provide a RISC OS-like interface on [Unix](/wiki/Unix "Unix") and [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux") systems. The separate work by RISC OS Ltd and Pace resulted in a [code fork](/wiki/Code_fork "Code fork"). This continued after the subsequent licensing agreement with Castle Technology, causing much community debate at the time.[[22]](#cite_note-osnews_what_it_would_take-22) The debate remains ongoing in 2011.

### RISC OS 4

In March 1999, a new company called [RISCOS Ltd](/wiki/RISCOS_Ltd "RISCOS Ltd") was founded. They licensed the rights to RISC OS from Element 14 (and eventually from the new owner, [Pace Micro Technology](/wiki/Pace_Micro_Technology "Pace Micro Technology"))[[23]](#cite_note-riscos.com-1999-23) and continued the development of OS 3.8, releasing it as *RISC OS 4* in July 1999.[[24]](#cite_note-riscos.com-1999-2-24)

Whilst the hardware support for Phoebe was not needed, the core improvements to RISC OS 3.80 could be finished and released. They included:

- a better file system, increasing the number of items in directory from 77 to approximately 88,000 and increasing the max length of a filename from 10 characters to 255[[25]](#cite_note-iconbar.com-1999-25)[[26]](#cite_note-marutan-26)
- a plugin based system configuration utility[[27]](#cite_note-marutan-wiki-27)
- a new screensaver API[[28]](#cite_note-marutan-wiki-2-28)
- an enhanced window manager[[29]](#cite_note-marutan-wiki-3-29)
- an updated interactive help application[[30]](#cite_note-marutan-wiki-4-30)
- a redesigned set of icons

According to the company, over 6,400 copies of RISC OS 4.02 on ROM were sold up until production was ceased in mid-2005.[[31]](#cite_note-riscos.com2005oct-31)

During 1999 and 2000, RISCOS Ltd also released versions of RISC OS 4 to support several additional hardware platforms, the [MicroDigital Mico](/w/index.php?title=MicroDigital_Mico&action=edit&redlink=1 "MicroDigital Mico (page does not exist)"),[[32]](#cite_note-chrisacorns1999-32) [MicroDigital Omega](/wiki/MicroDigital_Omega "MicroDigital Omega"), [RiscStation R7500](/w/index.php?title=RiscStation_R7500&action=edit&redlink=1 "RiscStation R7500 (page does not exist)")[[33]](#cite_note-chriswhyRiscStation-33) and the Castle Kinetic RiscPC.[[34]](#cite_note-iconbar.comKinetic-34) In 2003 a version of RISC OS 4 was released with support for the Millipede Graphics AlphaLock podule.[[35]](#cite_note-riscos.comRO4-35)

RISC OS 4 is also available for various hardware emulators for other operating systems. In September 2003 [VirtualAcorn](/wiki/VirtualAcorn "VirtualAcorn") released the commercial emulator [VirtualRPC](/wiki/VirtualAcorn "VirtualAcorn") which included a copy of RISC OS 4.02.[[36]](#cite_note-riscos.comVirtualAcorn-36) In December 2008 RISCOS Ltd made 4.02 available for non-commercial emulators for £5 in a product called Virtually Free.[[37]](#cite_note-riscos.comRO402-37)

### RISC OS Select and Adjust

In May 2001, the company launched *RISC OS Select*, a subscription scheme allowing users access to the latest OS updates. These upgrades are released as soft-loadable [ROM images](/wiki/ROM_image "ROM image"), separate to the ROM where the boot OS is stored, and are loaded at boot time.[[38]](#cite_note-riscos.comSelect-38) By providing soft-loads, physical ROM costs are eliminated and updates are able to be delivered with accelerated speed and frequency.[[39]](#cite_note-ROL_Select-39) It has also allowed the company to subsidise the retail price of ROM releases, which are generally a culmination of the last few Select upgrades with a few extra minor changes.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In May 2002 the final release of Select 1 was shipped that included;[[40]](#cite_note-riscos.comSelectCD-40)

- [DHCP](/wiki/DHCP "DHCP") client
- Multi-User support and logon
- Preview versions of new printer support and networking with [AppleTalk](/wiki/AppleTalk "AppleTalk")

In November 2002, the final release of Select 2 was shipped[[41]](#cite_note-select.riscos.com-41) that included;[[42]](#cite_note-select.riscos.com2002-42)

- Support for [CMYK](/wiki/CMYK "CMYK") sprites
- Hardware support for the scroll wheel on [PS/2](/wiki/PS/2_connector "PS/2 connector") mice
- Support for the window manager tools to be in a configurable order
- RiscStation hardware support is now in the kernel

In June 2004 the final release of Select 3 was shipped[[41]](#cite_note-select.riscos.com-41) that included:[[43]](#cite_note-select.riscos.comS3-43)

(The name was a play on the RISC OS GUI convention of calling the three mouse buttons 'Select', 'Menu' and 'Adjust'.) ### RISC OS Six

In October 2006, shortly after Castle Technology announced the Shared Source Initiative, RISCOS Ltd announced RISC OS Six, the next generation of their stream of the operating system.[[47]](#cite_note-newsfromriscos-47)

The first product to be launched under the RISC OS Six name, was the continuation of the Select scheme, Select 4.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] A beta-version of RISC OS 6, Preview 1 (Select 4i1), was available in 2007 as a free download[[48]](#cite_note-select.riscos.comRO6-48) to all subscribers to the Select scheme, both present subscribers and those whose subscription was renewed after 30 May 2004 but has since lapsed.

RISC OS Six brought portability, stability and internal structure improvements, including full 26/32-bit neutrality. It is now highly modularised, with legacy and hardware specific features abstracted, and other code separated for easier future maintenance and development.[[49]](#cite_note-select4changes-49) Teletext support, device interrupt handler, software-based graphics operations, the real-time clock, the mouse pointer, CMOS RAM support, and hardware timer support have been abstracted out of the kernel and into their own separate modules.[[49]](#cite_note-select4changes-49) Legacy components, like the VIDC driver, and obsolete functionality for the [BBC Micro](/wiki/BBC_Micro "BBC Micro") have been abstracted too.[[49]](#cite_note-select4changes-49) AIF and transient utility executable checking has been introduced also to protect against rogue software, while graphics acceleration modules may be provided for the SM501 graphics chip in the A9home and for [ViewFinder AGP podule cards](/wiki/Risc_PC#Podule "Risc PC").[[50]](#cite_note-ROL_RO6_new_features-50) In April 2008 the final release of Select 4 was shipped that included:[[51]](#cite_note-select.riscos.comRO64i4-51)

### RISC OS 5

*RISC OS 5* is a separate evolution by [Castle Technology Ltd](/wiki/Castle_Technology_Ltd "Castle Technology Ltd") based upon work done by Pace for their NCOS based set top boxes. RISC OS 5 was written to support Castle's [Iyonix PC](/wiki/Iyonix_PC "Iyonix PC") Acorn-compatible, which runs on the [Intel XScale](/wiki/Intel_XScale "Intel XScale") ARM processor. Although a wealth of software has now been updated, a few older applications can only be run on RISC OS 5 via an emulator called Aemulor, since the [ARMv5](/wiki/ARM_core "ARM core") XScale processor does not support [26-bit](/wiki/26-bit "26-bit") addressing modes. Likewise, RISC OS 5 itself had to be ported to run properly on the new CPU, and abstraction of the graphics and other hardware interfaces created, to allow it, for example, to use standard graphics cards, instead of Acorn's own VIDC chip.

In July 2003, Castle Technology Ltd bought the head licence for RISC OS from Pace Micro.[[55]](#cite_note-drobe.co.ukBuys-55)[[56]](#cite_note-Pace_2003-07-04-56)

### Shared Source Initiative

In October 2006, [Castle Technology Ltd](/wiki/Castle_Technology_Ltd "Castle Technology Ltd") announced a plan to release elements of RISC OS 5 under a source sharing license. The Shared Source Initiative (SSI) was a joint venture between Castle and [RISC OS Open Limited](/wiki/RISC_OS_Open_Limited "RISC OS Open Limited") (ROOL), a newly formed software development company, which aimed to accelerate development and encourage uptake of the OS. Under the custom dual license, released source was freely available and could be modified and redistributed without royalty for non-commercial use, while commercial usage incurred a per-unit license fee to Castle.

The SSI made phased releases of source code, starting in May 2007.[[57]](#cite_note-drobe.co.ukShared-57) By October 2008, enough source was released to build an almost complete Iyonix ROM image.[[58]](#cite_note-riscosopen.org2008-58) By late 2011, it was possible to build complete ROM images from the published sources; with the full source code available as [tarballs](/wiki/Tar_(computing) "Tar (computing)"), [CVS](/wiki/Concurrent_Versions_System "Concurrent Versions System"), or a web interface to the CVS archive.

In October 2018, the rights to RISC OS 5 were acquired by RISC OS Developments, and re-licensed under the [Apache 2.0](/wiki/Apache_2.0 "Apache 2.0") license.[[59]](#cite_note-theregisterROopensource-59) ROOL continues to maintain the source tree and co-ordinates an international developer community on a non-profit basis to support and encourage development.

Prebuilt images are available, as both stable releases and development "[nightly builds](/wiki/Nightly_build "Nightly build")".[[60]](#cite_note-ROM_image_releases-60)

Ports of RISC OS 5 are available for the [A7000/A7000+](/wiki/Acorn_A7000 "Acorn A7000"), [RiscPC](/wiki/RiscPC "RiscPC"), [RPCemu](/w/index.php?title=RPCemu&action=edit&redlink=1 "RPCemu (page does not exist)"), the [OMAP3](/wiki/OMAP#OMAP_3 "OMAP") [BeagleBoard](/wiki/BeagleBoard "BeagleBoard") and [derivatives](/wiki/Pandora_(console) "Pandora (console)"), [OMAP4](/wiki/OMAP#OMAP_4 "OMAP") [PandaBoard](/wiki/PandaBoard "PandaBoard") and PandaBoard ES, [OMAP5](/wiki/OMAP#OMAP_5 "OMAP") IGEPv5 and UEVM5432, [AM5728](/wiki/Sitara_ARM_Processor "Sitara ARM Processor") Titanium, the [Raspberry Pi](/wiki/Raspberry_Pi "Raspberry Pi"), and the XScale Iyonix.[[60]](#cite_note-ROM_image_releases-60)
